content: Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language through computational techniques. NLP development progressed from rule-based approaches through statistical methods to modern neural network approaches. Text processing begins with preprocessing steps: tokenization breaks text into words or subwords; normalization converts text to standard form (typically lowercase); and stemming or lemmatization reduces words to root forms. Statistical NLP techniques include bag-of-words representations that count word occurrences while ignoring order; TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) that weights words based on frequency and distinctiveness; and n-gram models that capture short sequences of adjacent words. Language modeling predicts the probability of word sequences, traditionally using n-gram statistics but now predominantly employing neural networks. Word embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe represent words as dense vectors in multidimensional space, capturing semantic relationships where similar words cluster together and relationships appear as consistent vector operations (like 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' â 'queen'). Modern NLP relies heavily on transformer architecturesâneural networks using attention mechanisms to process entire sequences simultaneously rather than sequentially. These underlie models like BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer), which are pre-trained on vast text corpora and fine-tuned for specific tasks. Common NLP applications include sentiment analysis (determining text emotional tone), named entity recognition (identifying people, places, organizations), machine translation, question answering, text summarization, and chatbots. Despite impressive capabilities, NLP systems still struggle with understanding context, resolving ambiguities, processing implicit knowledge, and generating reliably factual content.

scenario.title: Predictive Text Laboratory
scenario.content: Students develop and test language prediction systems that suggest text completions based on partial input. The simulation provides a messaging interface where students implement different NLP techniquesâfrom simple frequency-based approaches to advanced neural modelsâto predict what users will type next. The system includes datasets of varied text types (casual messages, formal writing, technical documentation) for training and testing prediction algorithms. Students can visualize how different models process language, showing token recognition, embedding spaces, attention patterns, or probability distributions over vocabulary. Interactive tools allow students to analyze model performance, identify prediction errors, and implement improvements. Challenge scenarios ask students to develop specialized prediction systems for specific domains or user preferences, teaching both fundamental NLP concepts and their practical application in everyday technology.

hypothesis.description: Students will implement text prediction systems by applying natural language processing techniques. They will analyze how statistical and neural approaches capture different aspects of language structure, and develop appropriate models for various text completion tasks.
